conventional_description: Urticaria, commonly known as hives, is a skin condition characterized by raised, red or skin-colored wheals that appear suddenly and are intensely itchy. They can range from a few millimeters to several centimeters in size and may join together to form larger plaques. The reaction is caused by the release of histamine and other chemicals from mast cells in the skin, often triggered by allergens, infections, stress, or physical stimuli like cold or pressure. Diagnosis is usually based on the appearance and history of the rash, though allergy testing may be done for persistent cases.
conventional_treatments: First-line treatment typically involves non-sedating antihistamines to block the histamine response and relieve itching. If these are not enough, doctors may add H2 blockers, short courses of oral corticosteroids, or in chronic cases, prescription medications like omalizumab (a biologic) or immunosuppressants. Identifying and avoiding triggers is also a key part of management.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, hives are understood as a battle between the body's protective Defensive Qi (Wei Qi) and an invading pathogen, most often Wind. Wind is the key culprit because it causes symptoms that appear suddenly, move around, and disappear just as quickly - exactly how hives behave. When Wind invades the skin, it disrupts the normal opening and closing of the pores, trapping Qi and fluids beneath the surface and producing the characteristic raised wheals.
But Wind rarely acts alone. It often teams up with Heat or Cold, which explains why some people get red, burning hives that worsen with warmth, while others get pale, less itchy wheals that flare in cold weather.
The digestive system also plays a central role: when the Spleen and Stomach are overloaded by rich, greasy, or spicy foods, they generate internal Dampness and Heat that can steam upward and erupt through the skin as bright, angry hives accompanied by bloating or loose stools.
In chronic cases, the picture shifts from external invasion to internal weakness. When Qi and Blood are deficient, the body's protective barrier is too weak to resist even mild triggers, leading to recurrent, pale hives that come and go with fatigue or stress. This is why TCM doesn't just treat the rash - it looks deeper to find the root imbalance, whether it's an acute excess of Wind-Heat, a lingering digestive issue, or a long-standing deficiency that needs to be rebuilt.
classical_quote: 「瘾疹者，由邪气客于皮肤，复逢风寒相折，则起风瘙瘾疹。」
classical_translation: "Urticaria (瘾疹) occurs when pathogenic Qi lodges in the skin, and then encounters Wind-Cold, which triggers the eruption of itchy wind wheals."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking about the color, temperature, and timing of your wheals, as well as any triggers and accompanying symptoms. These clues point toward one of the five main patterns behind urticaria. The tongue and pulse are then examined to confirm the diagnosis, because each pattern leaves its own signature on these internal signs.
If the wheals are bright red, feel burning hot, and flare up in warm weather or after hot food, Wind-Heat is likely. The tongue will be red with a thin yellow coating, and the pulse will feel floating and rapid. This pattern is very common in acute outbreaks that come on suddenly and itch intensely.
When the wheals are pale or light-red, worsen in cold air or after cold drinks, and may be accompanied by chills, the picture shifts to Wind-Cold. Here the tongue is pale with a thin white coating, and the pulse is floating and tight. The body is essentially reacting to a cold invasion that traps wind in the skin.
Digestive symptoms like abdominal pain, diarrhea, or constipation alongside bright red wheals suggest Damp-Heat in Stomach and Spleen. The tongue coating will be yellow and greasy, and the pulse will feel slippery and rapid. This pattern often follows a heavy, rich meal or long-standing digestive imbalance that generates internal heat and dampness.
Chronic or recurrent hives that are pale or skin-colored, with fatigue, dizziness, and a pale complexion, point to Qi and Blood Deficiency. The tongue looks pale with a thin coating, and the pulse is thin and weak. Here the body lacks the strength to defend itself, and minor triggers like stress or a slight breeze can set off an outbreak.
A severe acute attack with bright red, burning wheals that merge into large plaques, high fever, and chills signals Toxic-Heat. The tongue is red with a yellow or dry coating, and the pulse is flooding and rapid. This is a more intense heat pattern that requires immediate attention to cool the blood and clear toxins.

patterns.worse_with: Hot weather or warm rooms, Spicy, fried, or greasy foods, Alcohol, Emotional stress
patterns.better_with: Cool compresses or cool showers, Drinking mint or chrysanthemum tea, Rest in a cool, well-ventilated room, Avoiding spicy and greasy foods
patterns.why_this_happens: When Wind-Heat invades the body, it first attacks the skin and the Defensive (Wei) Qi that circulates at the surface. The Heat component makes the wheals red, hot, and intensely itchy, while the Wind nature causes them to appear and disappear suddenly. This acute pattern often follows exposure to warm wind, overheating, or spicy foods, and the rash worsens with warmth because Heat already inflames the skin.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red at tip and edges with a thin yellow coating. Pulse: floating (浮 fú) and rapid (数 shuò), easily felt at the surface.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind-Heat urticaria is driven by Heat and Wind trapped at the skin's surface. Heat-whether from the environment, food, or alcohol-adds fuel to the fire, making wheals redder and itchier. Cooling measures like cold compresses, cooling teas, and a calm environment help disperse that Heat, while avoiding spicy and greasy foods prevents further internal Heat from rising to the skin. Stress can stir up internal Wind, which is why emotional upset can also trigger or worsen the rash.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol, which add Heat to the body. Drink cooling teas like chrysanthemum, mint, or dandelion. Keep the environment cool and wear light, breathable clothing. A gentle rinse with cool water can soothe acute itching.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the digestive system is overloaded by rich, greasy, or spicy foods and alcohol, it can't process them properly. Dampness and Heat build up in the Stomach and Intestines, creating a kind of internal steam. This Damp-Heat then overflows into the skin, erupting as bright red, intensely itchy wheals that often flare up alongside abdominal bloating, pain, or bowel changes.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a thick, yellow, greasy coating, especially at the centre and root. Pulse: soggy (Ru) and rapid (Shu), often also slippery (Hua).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Greasy, spicy foods and alcohol directly generate Dampness and Heat, which are the root cause of this pattern. They overload the Spleen and Stomach, causing the internal steam that erupts on the skin. Hot, humid weather adds external Damp-Heat, making matters worse. On the other hand, light, cooling foods and regular bowel movements help the body clear Damp-Heat. Gentle exercise moves Qi, which is essential for transforming and draining Dampness.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat light, easily digestible meals. Steer clear of greasy, fried, or very spicy foods, and avoid alcohol completely during a flare-up. Cooling foods like mung beans, cucumber, and celery can help. Gentle daily movement like walking supports digestion and helps clear Dampness. Do not overeat; eat until you are about 70% full.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Qi and Blood are both insufficient, the body's protective Wei Qi becomes too weak to guard the skin against outside invaders like Wind. Blood deficiency also means the skin is not properly nourished, making it dry and reactive. The result is recurrent, pale or skin-colored wheals that appear when you are run down, tired, or stressed - a sign that your reserves cannot sustain a healthy barrier.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale body, may be thin or have teeth marks, thin white coating. Pulse: fine and weak (细弱 xì ruò).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Blood Deficiency leaves the body's exterior unguarded. Rest and nourishing food replenish the Qi and Blood that build a strong defensive shield, while overwork, poor diet, and stress drain those reserves further. Cold wind easily penetrates a weakened exterior, provoking hives. By strengthening the Spleen and Blood, the skin becomes less reactive and breakouts fade.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Build your reserves with warm, nourishing foods: bone broth, congee, dark leafy greens, red dates, and small portions of high-quality protein. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that tax the Spleen. Prioritize regular meals and adequate sleep. Gentle daily movement like walking or qigong helps circulate Qi without depleting it.

patterns.why_this_happens: Toxic-Heat is a severe, blazing form of internal Heat that flares up when external pathogens like Wind-Heat or Damp-Heat are not cleared and instead sink deeper, or when intense emotional upset and rich, greasy food generate fire poison. This fierce Heat surges into the blood and skin, erupting as bright red, burning wheals that merge into large plaques. The Heat also disturbs the body's thermostat and fluids, producing high fever, chills, intense thirst, and a restless, agitated mind.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with prickly thorns, dry yellow coating. Pulse: rapid (shu) and forceful (you li), often surging (hong) or slippery (hua).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Toxic-Heat is a fierce internal fire that consumes Yin and pushes Heat into the blood and skin. Cooling foods and cold compresses directly counteract the Heat, while rest and quiet conserve the body's Yin, which is being scorched. Spicy food, alcohol, and emotional stress add more Heat and stir up internal fire, making the wheals redder and more intense. Hot environments and overexertion further fan the flames, while gentle cooling and hydration help the body return to balance.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid all heating and stimulating foods - alcohol, coffee, spicy dishes, fried and greasy items, lamb, and shellfish. Embrace cooling, hydrating foods like cucumber, watermelon, mung bean soup, and plenty of room-temperature water. Rest in a cool, quiet space and avoid overheating; a lukewarm shower can calm burning skin without shocking it.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really stop hives?
faqs.answer: Yes, especially during an acute outbreak. Acupuncture helps calm the immune response, dispel Wind, and cool the blood - which can relieve itching and reduce the size of wheals within a single session. For chronic hives, regular weekly treatments over several weeks work to correct the underlying imbalance so that outbreaks become less frequent and less intense.

faqs.question: How long does it take for Chinese herbs to work on hives?
faqs.answer: Acute Wind-Heat or Wind-Cold hives often improve within a day or two of starting the right herbal formula. Damp-Heat and Toxic-Heat patterns may take a week or two to fully settle. Chronic hives rooted in Qi and Blood deficiency typically need 2-3 months of consistent herbal therapy to rebuild the body's reserves and break the cycle of recurrence.

faqs.question: Can I keep taking antihistamines while using Chinese herbs?
faqs.answer: Yes, it's generally safe to combine them. Many patients start TCM while still using their usual antihistamines and then gradually reduce the medication as symptoms improve. Always tell both your TCM practitioner and your doctor about everything you're taking so they can coordinate your care safely.

faqs.question: What foods should I avoid if I have hives?
faqs.answer: In TCM, spicy, greasy, and deep-fried foods, alcohol, shellfish, and excessive sugar are common triggers because they create internal Heat and Dampness. If your hives are linked to digestive symptoms, pay extra attention to how you feel after meals. Cooling foods like cucumber, mung beans, and chrysanthemum tea are often helpful, but the ideal diet depends on your specific pattern.

faqs.question: Why do my hives keep coming back even though I avoid triggers?
faqs.answer: Recurring hives often point to an underlying deficiency - your body's protective Qi may be too weak to fend off everyday exposures. TCM sees this as a Qi and Blood deficiency pattern, where the skin isn't properly nourished and the immune barrier is fragile. Simply avoiding triggers isn't enough; the constitution needs to be strengthened with herbs, diet, and acupuncture to stop the cycle.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe for hives during pregnancy?
faqs.answer: Yes, when guided by a qualified practitioner. Many acupuncture points and gentle herbal formulas are safe during pregnancy and can provide relief without the medications that are often restricted. However, certain herbs and strong points are avoided, so always make sure your practitioner knows you are pregnant before treatment begins.

research.title: The Efficacy and Safety of a Fixed Combination of Chinese Herbal Medicine in Chronic Urticaria: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Pilot Study
research.description: This pilot RCT tested a fixed herbal formula based on Xiao-Feng San in patients with chronic urticaria. After 12 weeks, the herbal group showed significantly greater reduction in urticaria activity scores than placebo, with no serious adverse events. The formula targeted Wind-Heat and Damp-Heat patterns, common in chronic hives.

research.title: Efficacy and safety of modified Xiao-Feng Powder in the treatment of chronic urticaria: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This meta-analysis pooled data from multiple RCTs on modified Xiao-Feng Powder (a classic formula for Wind-Heat and Damp-Heat urticaria). Results showed that the herbal formula significantly improved total effective rate and reduced recurrence compared to antihistamines alone, with a favorable safety profile.
research.periodical: Zhang, Y., et al. Chinese Medicine, 2022.
